condition.label: lumbar spinal stenosis
aliases: neurogenic claudication due to lumbar stenosis
condition.distinctions: This evidence principally concerns symptomatic stenosis causing neurogenic claudication; imaging-only stenosis, vascular claudication and postoperative states are not interchangeable.

scope.population: Adults at least 60, imaging-confirmed stenosis and neurogenic claudication; excluded cauda equina/prior stenosis surgery or fusion/severe competing walking conditions; Adults at least 50 with walking-limited neurogenic claudication; Lumbar spinal stenosis
scope.stage: Varies by source; acute/recent versus chronic and symptom irritability are explicitly retained. Unknown stage remains unknown.
scope.operativeStatus: Nonsurgical evidence predominates; no postoperative protocol approved or inferred.
scope.exclusions: Source-specific exclusions are applicability boundaries, not diagnosis-wide contraindications. Coexisting conditions and independently selected joint limits retain precedence.
scope.uncertainty:
- Ordinary training: for documented extension/standing-provoked claudication, shorten or modify that exposure and consider symptom-relieving supported/flexion-tolerant conditioning; mark this a symptom-based clinical inference (LSS-P1), not a global extension ban. Walking is not automatically excluded; it is an outcome and intervention in these trials.
- Supportive candidates: cycling, individually tolerable trunk/lower-limb strengthening, conditioning. Exact equipment/position and stage remain attributes. No diagnosis-wide numerical flexion angle, standing-duration cap, lifting limit or progression increment is established.
- Neurological deterioration/cauda-equina assessment cannot be replaced by a workout. Coexisting osteoporosis, radiculopathy, balance limitations and postoperative orders retain independent precedence.
- Currentness search found 2026 network meta-analysis PMC13145387 and a 2026 small feasibility RCT DOI 10.3390/app16104695; not fully extracted, no added rule based on them. No newer final exercise-specific guideline verified.

sources.population: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
sources.coInterventions: Many packages include supervision and manual/psychological components
sources.outcomes: Comer et al., 2024 (online 2023) systematic review/component analysis. DOI 10.1177/02692155231201048, PMID 37715644, PMC10829420; FT via XML. Thirteen trials, 1440 participants with neurogenic claudication; 23 exercise interventions, heterogeneous comparators. Supervision/flexion common; cycling, strengthening, stretching and psychological components more frequent in successful packages. Flexion itself appeared in both successful and unsuccessful programs. Component co-occurrence is not randomized proof of independent benefit or safety; no reliable supervision/dose conclusion. Supports considering tolerable fitness/strengthening within a multimodal plan, not prohibiting all extension or inferring every stretch is beneficial.
sources.uncertainty: Component co-occurrence does not identify causal effect; flexion occurs in successful and unsuccessful packages
sources.harms: Not comprehensively established at component level
sources.limitations: Component co-occurrence does not identify causal effect; flexion occurs in successful and unsuccessful packages Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.population: Adults at least 60, imaging-confirmed stenosis and neurogenic claudication; excluded cauda equina/prior stenosis surgery or fusion/severe competing walking conditions
sources.comparator: Medical care versus group exercise versus manual therapy/individualized exercise
sources.coInterventions: Medical management or individualized manual therapy according to arm
sources.outcomes: Schneider et al., 2019 RCT. DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.6828, journal FT. FT. 259 adults ≥60, imaging-confirmed LSS and neurogenic claudication; symptoms relieved by sitting/flexion among diagnostic signs. Six-week medical care, group exercise or manual therapy/individualized exercise; outcomes 2/6 months. Individualized package improved symptom/function scores more at 2 months; no between-group responder differences at 6 months. All groups improved walking. No serious treatment-related events; transient muscle soreness 54% individualized, 31% group exercise, 6% medical; all anticipated events resolved ≤48h. Excluded cauda equina, prior stenosis surgery/fusion and severe competing walking conditions; exclusions limit generalization. Symptom relief supports a tolerability-based posture adaptation, not proof extension damages tissue.
sources.uncertainty: Short-term between-group benefit did not persist at six months; package effects; diagnostic relief with sitting/flexion is not tissue-harm evidence
sources.harms: No serious treatment-related events; transient soreness 54% individualized, 31% group exercise, 6% medical; resolved within 48 hours
sources.limitations: Short-term between-group benefit did not persist at six months; package effects; diagnostic relief with sitting/flexion is not tissue-harm evidence Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.population: Adults at least 50 with walking-limited neurogenic claudication
sources.comparator: Home flexion/aerobic exercise plus advice versus advice/education
sources.outcomes: Comer et al., 2013 RCT. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0072878, PMID 24098633, journal FT. FT available text. Adults ≥50 with walking-limited neurogenic claudication; six-week home flexion/aerobic exercise plus advice versus advice/education. No significant symptom-severity benefit at 8 weeks (adjusted difference 0.06; 95% CI −0.19 to 0.31); no systematic sustained improvement; 12-month outcomes measured. No adverse events reported. Mean three contacts; post hoc severe-symptom subgroup not confirmatory. Important contrary evidence against claiming an app-delivered generic flexion program will reproduce supervised rehabilitation benefits.
sources.uncertainty: No significant primary benefit; severe-subgroup post hoc finding not confirmatory
sources.limitations: No significant primary benefit; severe-subgroup post hoc finding not confirmatory Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

protocol.dose: Six weeks; mean three professional contacts
protocol.supervision: Initial/contact PT support, predominantly home delivery

sources.outcomes: Whitman et al., 2006 RCT. DOI 10.1097/01.brs.0000241136.98159.8c, PMID 17047542. Abstract; full PDF located but not fully extracted. 58 people LSS, six-week manual therapy/body-weight-supported walking/exercise versus flexion/walking/subtherapeutic ultrasound. Recovery better with manual/exercise package (NNT 2.6 at six weeks); 62% versus 41% recovered at one year. Multi-component comparison cannot identify which exercise determines benefit, dose, or contraindications. Detailed harms unresolved.

proposedRules.statement: Candidate clinical inference: when assessed standing/extension exposure provokes claudication, adjust that exposure and investigate supported/symptom-relieving conditioning; do not apply a diagnosis-wide extension or walking ban.
